extracted.subtask_description: Statements, hypotheses, and proof techniques for weak and strong laws of large numbers, truncation arguments, triangular arrays, and Borel–Cantelli lemmas in a probability textbook setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence in probability (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yn converges to Y in probability if for all ε > 0, P(|Yn − Y| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the mode of convergence used in the conclusions of the weak-law theorems; it is used repeatedly to state limiting results for normalized sums and functions of random variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncorrelated family (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family of random variables Xi, i ∈ I with EXi^2 < ∞ is said to be uncorrelated if E(Xi Xj) = EXi EXj whenever i ≠ j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a weaker assumption than independence in variance-additivity results and weak laws; demonstrates that some limit theorems require only uncorrelatedness, not full independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variance additivity for uncorrelated variables (Theorem 2.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1, ..., Xn have E(Xi^2) < ∞ and are uncorrelated then var(X1 + ··· + Xn) = var(X1) + ··· + var(Xn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: expand E(Sn − ESn)^2, separate diagonal and off-diagonal terms and use uncorrelatedness to make cross-terms zero. This is a key computation ingredient for L2 convergence proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling of variance
rubrics_metrics.description: var(cY) = c^2 var(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic property used repeatedly to rescale sums and deduce L2 convergence of normalized sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: Lp to probability (Lemma 2.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p > 0 and E|Zn|^p → 0 then Zn → 0 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Chebyshev's inequality (Markov/Chebyshev type bound) with φ(x) = x^p; used to lift L2-convergence to convergence in probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: L2 weak law for uncorrelated variables (Theorem 2.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X1, X2, ... be uncorrelated with EXi = μ and var(Xi) ≤ C < ∞. If Sn = X1 + ... + Xn then Sn/n → μ in L2 and in probability as n → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: compute var(Sn/n) ≤ C/n → 0, so E(Sn/n − μ)^2 → 0; apply Lemma 2.2.2 to obtain convergence in probability. Special case: i.i.d. with EX^2 < ∞ yields same conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernstein polynomial / binomial approximation (Example 2.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Sn is sum of n independent Bernoulli(p) variables then Ef(Sn/n) equals the Bernstein polynomial fn(p) and Sn/n → p in probability; used to show fn → f uniformly for continuous f on [0,1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses P(|Sn/n − p| > δ) ≤ 1/(4 n δ^2) from variance bound p(1−p) ≤ 1/4 and Jensen's inequality to control Ef(Sn/n) − f(p). This demonstrates an application of the weak law to polynomial approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular arrays normalization result (Theorem 2.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Sn be any sequence of random variables with μn = ESn and σn^2 = var(Sn). If σn^2/bn^2 → 0 then (Sn − μn)/bn → 0 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No independence required for this trivial but useful result. It is used to analyze row sums of triangular arrays where bn is chosen to capture the relevant normalization scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak law for triangular arrays via truncation (Theorem 2.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each n let Xn,k, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, be independent. Let bn → ∞ and let n,k = Xn,k 1(|Xn,k| ≤ bn). Suppose (i) sum_{k=1}^n P(|Xn,k| > bn) → 0 and (ii) sum_{k=1}^n E(n,k^2) → 0. If Sn = sum_k Xn,k and an = sum_k En,k then (Sn − an)/bn → 0 in probability and b_n^{-2}(Sn − an) → 0 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show P(Sn ≠ n) → 0 by union bound on truncation events; then apply Chebyshev to the truncated sum using variance additivity. This theorem is the central truncation-based tool for weak laws without second-moment assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak law condition via tail weight (Theorem 2.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X1, X2, ... be i.i.d. with x P(|X1| > x) → 0 as x → ∞. Let Sn = X1 + ... + Xn and μn = E(X1 1(|X1| ≤ n)). Then Sn/n − μn → 0 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows by applying Theorem 2.2.11 with bn = n. The tail condition is necessary for existence of centering constants an so that Sn/n − an → 0; it is nearly equivalent to finite mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of moments via tail integrals (Lemma 2.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y ≥ 0 and p > 0 then E(Y^p) = ∫_0^∞ p y^{p-1} P(Y > y) dy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Fubini's theorem and the definition of expectation; used to relate integrability conditions to tail-decay conditions like x P(|X| > x) → 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak law under finite mean (Theorem 2.2.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1, X2, ... are i.i.d. with E|Xi| < ∞ and μ = EX1, then Sn/n → μ in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: truncation plus dominated convergence to control centering μn = E(X1 1(|X1| ≤ n)) → μ, then apply Theorem 2.2.12 to deduce convergence in probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truncation of a random variable (definition/operation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To truncate X at level M means  X = X 1(|X| ≤ M), i.e., equal to X on |X| ≤ M and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truncation is the main technical device used to reduce heavy-tailed variables to bounded ones so Chebyshev-type arguments can be applied; choice of truncation level bn is guided by trade-offs between moment control and tail probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Coupon collector normalization (application)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Xi i.i.d. uniform on {1,...,n} let Tn be time to collect all n coupons; then ETn ∼ n log n, var(Tn) ≤ const·n^2, and Tn/(n log n) → 1 in probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computations use geometric waiting times for new coupons, linearity of expectation, harmonic sum approximations, and Theorem 2.2.6 with bn = n log n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borel-Cantelli lemma (first) (Theorem 2.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If sum_{n=1}^9 P(An) < ∞ then P(An i.o.) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: consider N = sum 1_{An} and use Fubini to show EN < ∞ so N < ∞ a.s. Used frequently to convert summability of probabilities into almost-sure 'finitely many' conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequence characterization of convergence in probability (Theorem 2.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Xn → X in probability iff every subsequence X_{n(m)} has a further subsequence X_{n(m_k)} that converges almost surely to X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Borel-Cantelli to construct almost-surely convergent subsubsequences; this theorem is used to upgrade subsequential probability convergence to almost-sure statements in certain arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Borel-Cantelli lemma (Theorem 2.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If events An are independent and sum P(An) = ∞ then P(An i.o.) = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: bound P(∩_{n=M}^N A_n^c) ≤ exp(−sum_{n=M}^N P(An)) → 0, so P(lim sup An) = 1. This complements the first lemma for independent events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichotomy for heavy tails and occurrence infinitely often (Theorem 2.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1, X2, ... are i.i.d. with E|Xi| = ∞ then P(|Xn| ≥ n i.o.) = 1, hence P(lim Sn/n exists and is finite) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses Lemma 2.2.13 to relate infinite mean to non-summable tails, then applies second Borel-Cantelli. Shows E|X| < ∞ is necessary for strong law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise-independence strong-sum ratio (Theorem 2.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1, A2, ... are pairwise independent and sum P(An) = ∞ then (1 / sum_{m=1}^n P(Am)) sum_{m=1}^n 1_{Am} → 1 a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: let Xm = 1_{Am}; pairwise independence gives uncorrelatedness so var(Sn) ≤ ESn; apply Chebyshev to subsequence indexes nk with ET_{k} ≥ k^2 and use Borel-Cantelli to upgrade to a.s. convergence for the full sequence. Moral: pairwise independence + non-summability yields almost-sure frequency = expected frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong law under fourth moment (Theorem 2.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1, X2, ... are i.i.d. with EXi = μ and E X_i^4 < ∞ then Sn/n → μ almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: center to μ = 0, compute E(S_n^4) = O(n^2) and apply Chebyshev with fourth moments to get P(|Sn| > n ε) summable; conclude by Borel-Cantelli. Shows stronger moment assumptions give almost-sure convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etemadi strong law (Theorem 2.4.1) — pairwise independence + finite mean
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1, X2, ... are pairwise independent, identically distributed with E|Xi| < ∞ and EXi = μ, then Sn/n → μ almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truncation-based proof (Etemadi 1981) is indicated: truncation + pairwise independence suffices to obtain the strong law under only finite mean (weaker than requiring full independence). This is presented as the main strong law result to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tricks and asymptotic estimates used as criteria (harmonic sum bounds and elementary inequalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates such as sum_{m=1}^n 1/m ≥ ∫_1^n dx/x ≥ sum_{m=2}^n 1/m and bounds like 1 − x ≤ e^{−x} are used to compare sums and integrals and to relate expectations to logarithmic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These analytic inequalities are used throughout to derive asymptotic normalizations (e.g., n log n for coupon collector) and to control products of probabilities in Borel-Cantelli arguments.
